paragraphs.text: Again, an admonition to the solitary brothers by Mar Abraham of Nathpar, which he composed on the reason for the practices of the solitary life. To someone who asked him [?]
Because I have seen that you long to walk on the road that leads

to eternal life, the road our Savior Christ trod, O my beloved, I truly wished first to say a little about it to you, and then to fulfill your request in deed, as God grants. You, then, since the good plant of the love of virtue has been planted in you, have not only gladly listened to my words, but have also urged me to set down in writing what I said to you in person. I, being persuaded by your urging, have judged it good to set this matter out for you under headings, first stating its cause: why, when it seemed good to God that we should first be in this way of life and that afterwards He would give us another, He left some to be raised in this way of life and, by their conduct, to anticipate that other way of life from now on, as He wished [?]. First heading: that it is not for everyone to approach this way of life. Second heading: with what thoughts and deeds those who approach ought to approach. Third heading: once they have approached, how they ought to walk in it. Fourth heading: when temptations and battles befall them, what they should do. Fifth heading: if it happens that they fall, how they should rise. Sixth heading: what carefulness and diligence are required of those who walk in this road. But first [?], the cause of this way of life. I begin, then, with the help of your prayers, saying: at the beginning, the cause of this way of life, as I promised briefly above, I begin [thus]. If God had made us from the beginning not mortal and not passible, we would have possessed those good things irrationally, like beasts [?], and we would not have been able to delight in them, because we would not have been tested and taught. For it is from experience that we know them. Nor could knowledge of them have been fixed in us by nature, for [?] those things that are fixed by nature [are not perceived]. This can be seen clearly in irrational creatures [?], in [?] and in lilies, together with the rest of the [natural] things: they possess something of beauty [?], and because it is theirs by nature, they do not perceive it, and so they cannot delight [in it] [?].

For if He had given us knowledge of them by nature, could we have delighted in them with discernment? Rather, we would already have been of divine rank in our own presumption [?]. For He alone knows everything without experience and without learning, because His nature too is without beginning and without experience, and prior to all things without [?], and He knows everything at all times without trial and without learning. And again, if He had given us knowledge of them by nature, we would have known nothing else except what suffices for us [?], since we would not have contemplated His ordering or His manifold wisdom, which is in many kinds [of things], and, so to speak, we would have been deprived of much knowledge. But now, by His ineffable wisdom, He made us first mortal and passible, and we know that we are being trained in this [?]. For this reason He ordered this world in such a way that it might be a teacher to us about its Maker, through the opposition and changeableness of the natures in it and their changes from one into another. Our own nature He did not make simple, that is, soul alone or body alone, but composed it of two unequal parts, body and soul. And to each of the parts of our nature He gave something of its own: to the soul, together with knowledge and rationality, He gave love of good things; to the body, much susceptibility to the things that are pleasant. So that from here a war without peace and a continual affliction might arise for man within himself over the practice of the good, as the blessed Paul said: “For I delight in the law of God in the inner man; but I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive to the law of sin that is in my members.” This war without peace in the soul would establish a greater love for good things, so that the love of good things in the soul should not be without profit

— though it cannot be completely fulfilled here because of our passibility and mortality. He prepared for us another world, full of every kind of blessing, so that when we are there the practice of the good may be without affliction for us. This [world] was shown to us by our Savior Christ, who did not only teach us by His words but also showed it to us by deeds in His own person, and to all the believers in a type. Those, then, who have learned of the mysteries of the world to come and of the good things in it ought from now on to dwell on those good things in their minds. It is not that they despise these things as contemptible, but because their love for the things to come abounds in them, they leave the things that are seen, so that they may be drawn all the more into the love of the things to come. For the release of the thoughts from the things that are seen draws them to the love and longing for God, since they have no anchor [?] in the things that are seen, but in those that are to come and are unseen. For constant reflection on them sets the mind all the more ablaze. Let this suffice for the cause of this way of life. Now I begin the headings which we set out above. First heading: that it is not for everyone to approach this way of life. For many afflictions and battles meet one in it in various ways [?]. As for whoever wishes to walk on this road, I say that it is not for everyone to walk in it, because it is not everyone who can endure the pains and afflictions that meet one in it. Whoever wishes to walk in it must be able to show this [?], since its whole conduct is against nature; and whoever conducts himself against nature knows its afflictions. Yet this is not the only road that leads to the kingdom of heaven, nor is it this way of life alone that God requires [?] of all men. Rather, there are many paths and various roads. For a man can, according to his strength, choose for himself one path and walk in it. Our Life-giver Christ bears witness to this when He says in the parable of the seed: “That which fell on good ground and [yielded]

fruit, some a hundredfold, some sixty, and some thirty.” And again: “In my Father's house are many mansions.” By these He shows that the conduct of all men is not equal, nor are their rewards. But because this way of life is above nature, just as a man who stands continually before the king needs to take more care than all the king's other servants [?], so whoever is in this way of life [...] must keep himself not only from sins in deeds and actions and words, but must constantly have wakeful thoughts and a well-ordered mind. And how hard this road is, is plain: for unless a man is constantly watchful and on guard, he cannot be purified. And because not everyone is equal to it, I advise that not everyone should approach it; especially because of those [...] who, without knowing why they are leaving the world and approaching this way of life, approach it rashly, as if it were something ordinary. And while they think they are persevering, they do not persevere; and if a little affliction happens to reach them, they leave and flee, and cast off their first faith, as the herald Paul said. I have said these things not to hinder anyone who wishes to approach, but to counsel that he should not approach rashly, as if to something ordinary, but with knowledge and discernment. Second heading: with what thoughts and deeds [?] those who approach ought to approach. I counsel, O my lord, whoever wishes to walk on this road—since there are in it mountains and cliffs and robbers who plunder, and, so to speak, it is a narrow and constricted road, full of affliction [...] and pains; and it is also like a pool full of water in which there are [?] and serpents, which take the water out of the pool and leave it bare [?]—I counsel, therefore, that whoever wishes to walk in it should enter it with knowledge and testing. And before everything, the study of the divine scriptures is necessary for him, which [?] for him to tread the road and to guide [him]. And it can

show him the signs and tokens of confidence. With the scriptures a man finds provisions that bring him to the end of his journey; he drives away from himself a foolish mind and a distracted thought, and the hearing of unprofitable words, in which those who are deficient in knowledge take pleasure. Some say that the study of the scriptures breeds arrogance and boasting. But let whoever says this know that if a purging medicine works in this way, what will a whole basket of dates do [?]. I have said this not denying that the study of the scriptures becomes a cause of boasting for many, but [meaning] that those are like a man whose [stomach?] is sick, for whom the purge that is given to him works in this way [?]. For an evil [?] man, whose paths are not straight, finds all his inquiry twisted and crooked; the thoughts of his aim are not restrained and pure, and his deeds are not [?]. Rather, let him heal this mind and remove it [?] from himself. And let him know that just as no one can cross a great sea without a ship or a boat, and just as no one can go into a fierce battle and come out unharmed when he is stripped [of armor] or [?] and does not even know how to shoot an arrow, so no one can enter this battle untrained and come out unscathed. For from the books he learns which things are sins and what righteousness is. He joins battle with the evil one, and from them he learns his evil arts, which are continually prepared against us. From them he is equipped to loose arrows against him. From them he comes to know which is his road and where it leads, whether to the right or to the left. From them [come] those [weapons?] which [?] in it. From them he is renewed, so that he may be as wise as the serpent and as simple as the dove. And greater than all these: from them he learns the true faith, which is rightly confessed in the Trinity of the worshipful hypostases, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, one power that holds all things and governs all.

I have said these things, O my lord, not cutting off hope in the help of divine grace. But understand what I am saying: if there is anyone who, without the study of scripture, has excelled in good works toward God, consider this too: if without study he was kept safe, how much more would he have been with study! Even though grace helps in every way, I keep to the order of the examples [?]. And let [your mind] meditate constantly on the world and its changes, looking at the labors and afflictions its inhabitants endure; rising in thought to kings and descending to beggars, and seeing that they all fall into one and the same affliction: kings because of their dominions, rulers because of themselves [?], the rich because of their wealth, the poor because of their want. And who can recount its troubles and distresses, and how it lies open to every evil? It grew rich and was exalted; it grew poor and was envious; it hungered and thirsted; it was sated and grew wanton; it ruled and was cast down; it was puffed up and blasphemed. Its joys do not last; its punishments are without end; its pleasure lasts the twinkling of an eye; its groans are unending; its afflictions are without number; and its troubles have no rest [?]. Its inhabitants are afflicted in body and afflicted in soul: the rich by cares and the poor by toil; thieves as they wait to steal, and watchmen as they keep their night watches. The rich look to be bribed, and the poor contrive to bribe. If a man gets treasures [...] to rejoice in them and be at ease, his work turns into distressing affliction: he is wakeful and afraid; he pants after the remedy and is shaken [?]. For its sake [he runs] on the roads; for its sake he goes down to the sea; for its sake he is killed by robbers; for its sake he climbs mountains; for its sake there is [the greed] of mammon, even when he is full [?]. [...] I do not know [?]. And greater than all: the thing that is thought sweeter than all is the most distressing. Ponder these things constantly, O my lord, so that the love of the world may be blotted out [?] from your mind. These things I have said as to the weak. Turn, my lord, and look at the sons of

[...] who, lo, are [?]; and at the merchants [?] who, lo, wander about in the shops [?]. [...] the flock [?] of Christ, who, lo, quarrel over a boundary. Look at [...] their [?] who, lo, wander in [?]. O men, why the blindness of your discernment? His father was afflicted and left [it], and lo, his son has taken up his affliction. His father went and drowned, and lo, his son runs after him. What did your father gain from his affliction, O fool, that you walk in his way? Turn, my lord, and look at those who love God. Those [others] are distressed when they are rich; these [are glad] when they give away. Those are grieved when they receive crowns [?]; these rejoice when they are struck, and when they are persecuted they are glad. Those mourn when they reign; these conquer when they are slain. Be mindful, then, in your soul of all the temptations, so that when they meet you, you do not leave and flee. Keep far away from all bodily possessions [?], so that the cares over them do not hinder you from walking on your road. Despise bodily concerns, so that they do not confuse your paths and [?]. Approach, armed with all these things; and approach in confidence to your Creator, casting all your care upon Him. Do not be slack, but set your will manfully, like a warrior, both your hands supported on the armor of righteousness on the right and on the left, that is, in things that distress and in things that gladden, in those who praise and in those who [despise], without your thoughts being divided: “If I can, [well]; and if not, I will turn back”—lest the evil one confound you and carry you off like a captive. And remember constantly what is written: “Do not approach it with two hearts”; and that other saying: “If you approach the fear of God, prepare your soul for every temptation.” Lay your foundation as on rock, on humility. Third heading: once they have approached, how they ought to conduct themselves. If, then, you have approached, O my lord, armed, and have laid your foundation on the rock of truth, and armed your mind like a warrior

and like a soldier and a strong man, like a shepherd and like a reaper, carrying the yoke of your Lord and bearing your cross on your shoulder; and if you have cast the world and its desires away from you, and loved our Lord and His glory, and become poor in all things that are seen, so that you may become an heir of the good things to come; and if, though mortal in body, you are mingled in your conduct with the companies of the watchers, and, though on earth, you are like one who is in heaven [...] in your ways—then make yourself from now on dead to all things that are seen. Set before your eyes as your goal purity of soul, for the sake of which all the commandments of God were given and toward which they all look; and in every way let your conduct look toward it. Do not neglect the great things, nor [stop short] in fulfilling the small ones; but begin with the small, so that you may reach the great. Let your fasting be in measure and discernment, knowing that God does not seek the outward deprivation of [?] for its own sake, but [seeks] the mind, for the sake of [?], that is, as the subduing of the passions of desire. For it is not possible for a man to order his thoughts otherwise unless he restrains his desires. Just as an unbridled horse cannot be subdued without a bridle and a halter, so the body cannot be made subject to the soul unless its desires are first subdued. Along with the fasting of the body, acquire also the fasting of the soul—that is, fast from envy and hatred, which are the mother of many sins; for from them are born murderous envy and destructive anger [?] and all the other sins—so that it may be a figure of the fast after the resurrection, in which we shall be entirely without sins. Let your service of prayer also be in measure and discernment, knowing that God is not pleased by a multitude of psalms but by a watchful mind that gazes on Him as on a great wonder. Do not seek to have this mind all at once and on the spot, for it is attained only little by little and through great labors. I have said these things so that your mind may not be occupied with the service of psalms alone, but mingled with the contemplation

of God, even if not completely. For just as a man cannot walk a road in haste without having set himself the goal of where he is going, so a man cannot reach this wonder of God—which comes as by stages [?]—unless he has first set it before himself as his goal. If distraction comes upon you while you stand in service, and you gather your thoughts and they will not be gathered, sit down. Move yourself to weeping or to sighing, saying in your heart: even if [I have fallen short] in one practice, by another I [draw near] to God [?]. And do not be troubled in your mind and say, “I have not served.” For, as I said, God is not pleased by the recitation of psalms alone. You know this too: the psalms were appointed for this reason, that by the repetition of the great words in them your mind might be roused and turn to God. In every way, my brother [?], be careful not to give affliction room in your mind for a long time, lest it bring you to despair, and despair bring you out of your labors. If you are troubled, let your gloom be in measure. If you are sitting in stillness and many and various thoughts rise against you, do not say, “I am idle,” and so let gloom overcome you and go out of your cell. Rather, hope for hope, and remember that after affliction comes joy, and after toil, rest. Love stillness, then, above everything; this brings you to purity of soul, if you wish. For just as, as I said, the sea cannot be crossed without a ship or a boat, so a man cannot reach purity of soul without stillness. And just as a man cannot see his face in water unless it is calm, so a man cannot see his faults and scour them away without stillness. And just as a man cannot enter a city fortified with great and strong walls except by going in through its gates, so a man cannot reach

purity of soul unless he scours away all its blemishes. Its very name, “purity of soul,” makes known the cleansing from all blemishes. And just as a man cannot [see] his face in a silver mirror unless it has been polished, so a man cannot reach the vision and the wonder of God unless he first polishes all the blemishes from his soul. Be mindful of these things always. Do not confine your conduct to bodily hardship and endurance and the repetition of psalms, when the divine vision and constant reflection on His greatness are not mingled with them. For just as he who shepherds the wind gains nothing, as the saying [?] goes, so too is he who confines his conduct to these things. I say this not that those things should not be done, but that these should be done along with those. For those are outward, in the body only; but these are inward, in the mind and in the love of the soul. Adorn yourself, then, with the inward things: the subduing of evil passions and the [armor?] of the love of God. Again I counsel you: be constantly at the door of the cell of a man pure of soul, by whom you may be instructed [?]. Fourth heading: if battle rises against them, how [they should act]. You, O my lord, if battle rises against you, do not be troubled and shaken, but support your mind with endurance, without which not one of those who fear God was proved and pleased Him. Bring to mind the afflictions of the prophets, the sufferings of the martyrs, the persecutions of the righteous: some of them were stoned, some were sawn in two, some were killed, some were cut to pieces, some were burned, and some poured out [their blood] without [?]; and, so to speak, there is not one of them who received his crown without endurance. Remember also Paul, who cries out that with all these [is needed] endurance, without which no one will see our Lord. Remember those who loved God: not one of them finished his course in ease, but in various afflictions. Along with these, bring to mind those who are in the world: not one of them attains the fulfillment of his desire without affliction. Some of them fall into seas,

[...] some of them climb mountains for the sake of gold; some of them walk on rough roads for the sake of passing wealth and empty glory. And if these [do] thus, how much more do those who pursue eternal wealth, imperishable treasures and pleasure that does not cease need endurance of the pains and afflictions that befall them [...], clothed in the breastplate of faith, by which they can quench all the burning arrows of the evil one. Remember that faithful word of our Savior Jesus Christ: “By your endurance you will gain your souls.” And again He said: “He who endures to the end, he shall live.” Bringing these things to mind, O my lord, stand manfully and do not fear. Cast your care upon the Lord, and He will deliver you. Give yourself to prayer constantly, without ceasing. And if you are not heard quickly, [know that] for your profit God leaves you, so that your endurance may be made known—not to Him, but to us and also to the host [?] of the demons. If a war of thoughts rises against you, know that if you do not seek [them], it is like a stranger [passing by] [?]. If a war of passions rises against you, go to brothers who are known [to you] and receive [counsel]. Do not be ashamed before others when they show you [your wounds?] [?]; but move yourself to prayer and ask of God, and do not quickly leave and flee. Above all, in your temptations do not leave your cell. For just as a man who, because of a small affliction that befalls him, would waste the labor of a whole year, so is he who has kept stillness for a long time and, in this small battle—after which he is about to reach great rest and firm peace—leaves and flees. In your temptations be constantly mindful of your vows [?]. Be mindful constantly also of the good things and the torments to come, so that reflection on them may lighten for you the multitude of afflictions. And, so to speak, remember that today there is affliction and tomorrow rest. And quickly

you will be strengthened by the hidden power of God [...]. Fifth heading: if it happens that they fall, how they should rise. If it happens that you fall, O my brother, do not stand still in despair and turn back to the world. Remember that your Lord is merciful and receives the erring who repent. Do not forget that faithful word of our Life-giver Christ: “I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.” Remember the parable of the prodigal son, in which He shows the mercies of God: how He receives sinners when they repent and shares His good things with them. And again the parable of the widow who had lost her coin, how she rejoiced over it. And again the sheep that was lost. And again: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are badly sick.” And again remember Paul, who cries out: “Faithful is the saying, that Jesus Christ came into the world to give life to sinners, of whom I am the first; so that in me first Jesus Christ might show all His long-suffering.” And again what was said by our Lord Himself: “If your brother offends against you seven times in a day, and seven times in a day turns back to you and says to you, ‘I repent,’ receive him.” Bring forward testimonies [?], and from among them, of deeds: first of blessed David; then come to the preachers of the New [Covenant], and you will find among them deniers like Simon, tax collectors like Matthew, and persecutors like Paul. By these God showed that He opens the door of repentance to sinners. Remember that sinful woman whose debts were forgiven through her tears; and that one of the Corinthians, who, though he had fallen into a great and grievous sin, was forgiven through a little repentance, and they even restored him to his former rank. But why do I confine my words to small things? Look at the whole church: it was gathered from nowhere else than from erring pagans and from Jews who crucified [Christ]. Remembering these things, O my lord, stand firm in confidence in the mercy of your Maker, not divided in your mind and saying: “I will not be forgiven; and even if I am forgiven, to my former rank

I will not attain,” lest that [division] cast you into the pit of despair, that is, into sins worse than the first. Rather, bring to mind blessed David: after he had received forgiveness for his folly [...] the prophet, what does he cry out and say? “Lord, do not rebuke me in Your anger, nor chastise me in Your wrath.” As if [he were saying]: because of my sin which I committed, O my lord, I deserve [...]; I deserve to be rebuked—not asking [not to be rebuked], but that he might be rebuked and chastised not in wrath and [anger]. Again in another psalm he says: “How long, Lord, will You forget me forever?” That is: I deserve to be forgotten for the sins I committed, but I ask that You not forget me forever. And again in another psalm: “My wounds stank and festered because of my folly; I was greatly [troubled] [?].” By these he shows that his sin pursued him even after it had been forgiven. And again: “Lord, all my desire is before You, and my groaning is not hidden from You,” as if he were saying, “Forgive me my sins.” Be mindful of these things in your heart, O my lord, if it happens that you slip through the weakness of nature and fall. And when you have risen, hold fast to the commandments of our Lord with all your heart, and He will help you. Sixth heading: what carefulness and diligence are required in this way of life. Concerning carefulness and diligence, O my lord, I think many words are not needed, because their profit is well known. But so that it may be known how much they are needed for this way of life, I will say a few words about them, speaking first of the losses that come from negligence and laziness, from the experience of which it will be known how much carefulness and diligence are required. I make the beginning of my words the words of the wise man [?], who spoke thus: “My son, if you sleep a little, and slumber a little, and lay your hand on your breast a little, then poverty will come upon you, and want will overtake you like a strong man.” At the head [...]

…let it be our concern to explain these words [?], so that they may become known to us. Human nature, then, O my lord, loves ease. When the will gives nature a little room, nature at once completes what is its own. Just as when you give a lame man your hand he can walk, so, if the will grows a little slack [and gives] room to nature, nature completes what is its own. As the wise man said here: “If you are a little slack and give room to sleep”, that is, to nature, “then nature completes what is its own.” That is what “you sleep” means. And once nature has had its fill of this one kind of thing, it inclines to another. That is what “a little you place your hand on your breast” means. Then it drives this on, and then poverty comes upon us, so that want overtakes you. This is what he meant: by the elegance of his words he pointed to sluggish sloth. That is, you will be in want of every good thing, and if you have anything, you will lose it. He spoke well of “a diligent man”, meaning diligent in idleness and negligence. In all these words the point of his saying is about the foolish man. You are foolish [?], for although you were able to be careful and diligent in good things, [?]. Have you seen what this wise man said about negligence, diligence and carefulness? Hear what he says again in another place: “I passed by the field of a lazy man, and by the vineyard of a man lacking sense. It had all grown up and was filled with thorns and thistles, and brambles covered its face.” Such is the man who acquires a vineyard of righteousness and, through his negligence and lack of diligence, many thorns spring up in it, which come upon him without his knowing. [?] like thorns acquired in it. Or who does not know how many [cities?] were snatched from the hands of their lords the kings by their enemies? How many houses of men were burned with fire, how many thousands of ships sank, through carelessness, negligence and lack of diligence? Remember these things and things like them, O my lord. Do not trust in the success of your past labors and say, “From now on there is no need for”

“vigilance on my part.” Who will remember the blessed David, a just and righteous man, how through a [little] negligence that came over him in the sight of his eyes he slipped and fell into a great sin, and not be afraid that he too may be shaken, and so be vigilant at all times? If you wish to escape, O my lord, hear my words and you will find rest for your soul. Set watchmen continually over the gate of your thoughts, so that you do not think of things that are not according to the will of God. Set watchmen over your mouth, so that it does not speak an evil word against your brothers. Set watchmen over your eyes, so that they do not look wantonly; and over your hearing, so that your ears do not hear foolish voices and your thoughts are not troubled. Weigh your words in a balance, my lord: which ones are needed, and when it is needful to speak. If you keep these things, O my lord, you will find rest for your soul and for those who know you. And keep this small example in your memory, O my lord. A farmer ought not to trust that his seed has come through unharmed until it is [gathered] into the storehouses. In the same way a man ought not to trust in his virtues until the time of his death. For it is like seed: if it has had rain and sprouted, the [locust] comes and eats it; and if it escapes the [locust], [?] hail beats it down; and if it escapes the hail, [?] torrents come and sweep it away. So it is with a man who lives this way of life. If he gets away and escapes from lust, the love of money meets him. If he happens to escape the love of money, demons attack. And if he again [escapes] from the demons, empty glory meets him, or destructive pride. For this reason, O my lord, unless a man is wakeful and watchful, he is tossed about and [?] as if by [?]. Meditate on these things continually. Here is another, additional word: do not read when you are weary, and do not read like someone who just reads,

but as one who means to put it into practice. Read, and be diligent in what belongs to the Lord, so that no kind of pride takes you captive, which over [?] [prayer?] [?], how he pursued [the stone(?) of the one who prays, and ?] [?] and careful [in his ?] [?]. Be diligent in prayer, and be [?] for you, and remove from you [?]. Keep vigil by night and by day, and do not [?] cut yourself off. I will show you the kinds of prayer. [?] offer petition, and at the time when you are provided for [?] by God, give thanks to God [?] joyful [?]. Offer praise [?] with discernment [?]. But, my beloved, [?] people in idleness and negligence [?] God, and who [?] and in [?] asks [?] his petitions, because he does not [?] and believes [?] in prayer while he is not pure [from all wickedness] and from every blemish. And [?] his offering purely [?] receive it well. [Let him beware] lest anything be found in him [for which it would be rejected.] For prayer is an offering, [and a precious ?]. [So] be diligent in it, my sons, and labor in it [?] all your prayers. [That] prayer which our Lord taught [?] [?] and the voices and their distinctions [?] my beloved. [Do not] suppose that prayer is words, and that it is [?] learned [by] words. Hear, rather, from our Lord that true [prayer] is not learned and is not perfected by instruction and by the repetition of words. For you are not praying to a man, that you should recite elaborately composed words before him. For he to whom you send the movements of prayer is spirit. Pray to him in the spirit, as befits him. And a place is not needed for one who prays to God perfectly, nor speech of the tongue. Our Lord said: “The hour is coming when neither on this mountain nor in [Jerusalem]

will you worship the Father.” He also taught that no place is needed any longer: “Those who worship God must worship in spirit and in truth.” And when he teaches us why prayer should be like this, he says: “For God is spirit.” And spiritually, and not [?].
